152.subtitle: Two treasuries of savour, and then five names beginning in p

commentary.meaning: Nine names in two lines, which is crowded even for this hymn, and crowded because the second line is built of very short words. The first line finishes an argument the previous verse began. There, kalā appeared as a garland and rasa appeared inside the word sāmarasya; here both come back as the whole subject. She is the hoard where the kalās are kept, she is the art by which poetry is made, she knows rasa, and she is the store where rasa is kept. The line is framed by two different words for treasury, with the two words for skill and savour held between them, so that the sense runs from container to contents and back to container. Then the second line drops the vocabulary of connoisseurship entirely and gives five plain names in a row, all beginning in p: she is well-fed, she is ancient, she is to be worshipped, she is a lotus, her eyes are lotuses. After four names about the refinement of taste the verse ends by looking at her face. That is not a change of subject. It is the demonstration.
commentary.history:
Nidhi is a buried hoard — the word used for the legendary treasures of Kubera, and for anything laid down and kept. Kalānidhi, treasury of digits, is also one of the ordinary poetic names for the moon in classical Sanskrit, since the moon is where the sixteen kalās are stored and paid out one a night. The name therefore arrives with a second meaning already attached, and it does so directly after the previous verse called her kalāmālā, a garland of the same digits. Grammatically it is worth noticing that nidhi is a masculine noun and stays masculine here, standing in apposition to her rather than being feminised. The consequence shows up in the litany of individual salutations, where the form is kalānidhaye namaḥ.

Kāvya is what a poet makes, and kalā in this compound has slid from its lunar and fractional senses over to its other career as art or practised skill — one of the sixty-four accomplishments a cultivated person was expected to have. To call her the art of poetry is a stronger claim than calling her its patron. Sarasvatī is the goddess who grants poetry; this name says that the craft itself, the thing that happens when words are made to carry more than they state, is her. The Śrīvidyā tradition has a long attachment to this idea and a founding anecdote for it in the Saundaryalaharī, where a child is given her breast to drink and grows up to outdo the accomplished poets — a story attached in different regions to different figures, which is a good sign that what mattered was the claim rather than the biography.

Rasa has already been discussed in the previous verse under sāmarasya, and the two names here take it in its two most developed technical directions. Rasajñā, one who knows rasa, is in ordinary Sanskrit also a noun for the tongue, the organ that knows taste; the name thus sits on the boundary between the physical and the aesthetic senses of the word without choosing. Behind the aesthetic sense stands Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and its famous formula that rasa arises from the conjunction of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states — a sentence so compressed that the entire subsequent history of Sanskrit literary theory can be read as a quarrel about how to construe it. The quarrel matters here because its central question is whether rasa is in the work, in the actor or in the audience, and rasajñā answers by locating the knowing in her.

Śevadhi, the second word for treasure, is the older and rarer of the two; it belongs to the Vedic layer of the language and carries the sense of a store that is not depleted by being drawn on. Rasaśevadhiḥ therefore does not simply repeat kalānidhiḥ at the other end of the line. It says that savour is the sort of thing that can be given away indefinitely, which is the standard position of the aestheticians about rasa and the standard position of the theologians about her.

The second line changes register completely. Puṣṭā, from √puṣ, means nourished, thriving, filled out — the word used of well-fed cattle and healthy crops. It belongs to the oldest stratum of Indian goddess vocabulary, the language of the Śrī Sūkta, where prosperity is described in agricultural terms and requested in the same breath as beauty. Purātanā is formed from purā, in former times, with the suffix that also gives sanātana, everlasting: not merely old but belonging to the time before. Pūjyā is a gerundive from √pūj, to honour, and it joins a small series of such forms running through this hymn — ārādhyā appeared in the verse three back and again in the verse two back, each time with a named worshipper attached. Here there is no worshipper named, and the effect of the bare gerundive is to generalise: not worshipped by heroes or by a particular Bhairava, simply to be worshipped.

Puṣkara is a word of very wide range. It is the blue lotus, and it is also water, a pond, the sky, the bell of a drum and the tip of an elephant's trunk; it is the name of a famous lake and pilgrimage town in Rajasthan. In the Śrī Sūkta the goddess is called puṣkariṇī, lotus-bearing or pond-like, in the same verse in which she is called puṣṭi, nourishment — the two words of this line standing side by side in a hymn a great deal older than this one. Puṣkarekṣaṇā, the last name, is a straightforward bahuvrīhi with the join of a and ī producing e: she whose eyes are lotuses. Lotus-eyed is among the most worn epithets in Sanskrit, applied to almost every deity and most heroes, and its placement here is what redeems it. Four names have just described a faculty of discrimination so refined that it has taste itself in storage. The verse closes by turning that faculty into a pair of eyes and looking back.
commentary.practice:
The alliterative organisation noted in the previous verse continues here and is now unmistakable. The first line pairs two k-names with two r-names; the second line gives five names in succession all beginning with p, which is the same organising principle that governed the second line of the verse four back. Over these several verses the composer is working with two shapes only — half-lines filled by one or two long compounds, and half-lines packed with short names bound by a shared initial — and the practical value of noticing this is that it converts a formless list into something with a rhythm you can anticipate.

The first line has three visarga-final and jñā-containing hazards. Kalānidhiḥ and rasaśevadhiḥ both end in -dhiḥ: an aspirated dental dh, a short i, then the visarga, which in careful recitation carries a faint echo of the preceding vowel. Do not let the aspiration of dh collapse into a plain d, and do not let the short i lengthen. Rasajñā has the jña cluster, whose regional pronunciations differ legitimately — gya, dnya or jña with both consonants sounded — and the only wrong answer is a bare j. Kāvyakalā has vy, a labiodental v with a palatal y following immediately.

Both -dhi names are i-stem nouns, and neither takes the -āyai ending. For individual salutation they are kalānidhaye namaḥ and rasaśevadhaye namaḥ. This is now the fourth verse running in which at least one name declines against the pattern the ear has learned, and the lesson is worth stating plainly: in this stretch of the hymn the dative should be checked and not guessed.

The second line is a pronunciation drill disguised as a list. Puṣṭā, puṣkarā and puṣkarekṣaṇā all contain ṣ, the retroflex sibilant, which is made with the tongue-tip curled back and is distinct both from the dental s of purātanā and from the palatal ś. In puṣṭā the ṣ is followed by a retroflex ṭ, so the tongue is already in position and simply stops; in puṣkarā it is followed by a guttural k, which requires the tongue to travel from the roof of the mouth to the back in one motion. Saying the two names alternately, slowly, is the best available exercise for separating the three sibilants. Puṣkarekṣaṇā adds kṣ, a guttural k with a retroflex ṣ, which is a single cluster and not two syllables.

Watch the vowel in pūjyā. It is long — pū, not pu — and it is the only one of the five p-names in the line that has a long vowel in its first syllable. Under speed the line tends to flatten into five identical openings, and that one long ū is the thing that keeps it from being a stutter.

What the verse asks of the reciter is a small adjustment of attitude at the halfway point. The first line is about connoisseurship, about knowing and storing what is fine, and it is easy to chant in a manner that matches — deliberate, savouring, slightly self-admiring. The second line will not support that. It is five short words about being well-fed, being old, being owed reverence, and having a face, and it should be said plainly. The verse has arranged its own correction, and the correction only works if the second line is not performed.

crossReferences.deva: तव स्तन्यं मन्ये धरणिधरकन्ये हृदयतः पयःपारावारः परिवहति सारस्वतमिव । दयावत्या दत्तं द्रविडशिशुरास्वाद्य तव यत् कवीनां प्रौढानामजनि कमनीयः कवयिता ॥
crossReferences.iast: tava stanyaṃ manye dharaṇidharakanye hṛdayataḥ payaḥpārāvāraḥ parivahati sārasvatam iva | dayāvatyā dattaṃ draviḍaśiśur āsvādya tava yat kavīnāṃ prauḍhānām ajani kamanīyaḥ kavayitā ||
crossReferences.translation: Daughter of the mountain, I take your milk to be an ocean of Sarasvatī's own water flowing out from your heart; for the Dravidian child, having tasted what you in your compassion gave him, became a poet lovely even among poets of the first rank.
crossReferences.relevance: The tradition's own account of what kāvyakalā means in practice. Poetic skill here is not a gift she bestows on a suitable candidate; it is her substance, taken in by a child too young to have earned anything. The identity of the draviḍaśiśu is disputed — the verse has been attached to Śaṅkara himself and to the Tamil saint Jñānasambandhar, among others — and the fact that the story survives without a settled subject suggests that the claim about poetry mattered more than the biography.

crossReferences.source: Śrī Sūkta, the verse beginning ārdrāṃ puṣkariṇīṃ (13 in the common numbering; recensions differ, and some transmit a near-duplicate of it)

crossReferences.translation: Moist, full of lotuses, thriving, tawny-gold, garlanded with lotuses, shining like the moon, made of gold — bring Lakṣmī to me, knower of all that is born.
crossReferences.relevance: Two of the words in the second line of this verse, puṣṭi and puṣkara, standing together in a hymn far older than the sahasranāma, in the same order and to the same purpose. It shows that puṣṭā and puṣkarā are not casual epithets but a very old formulaic pairing of nourishment and the lotus, and it supplies the register the second line is written in: agricultural, unembarrassed about prosperity, and concrete.

crossReferences.source: Nāṭyaśāstra of Bharata, chapter 6, the prose rasasūtra (editions place it at different points within the chapter)
crossReferences.translation: Rasa comes about from the conjunction of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states.
crossReferences.relevance: The sentence that made rasa a technical term and the one every later theorist had to interpret. Its unresolved question — where the rasa actually occurs, in the drama, in the performer or in the person watching — is precisely what rasajñā settles by naming a knower rather than a location. Reading the sūtra also explains why rasaśevadhiḥ can call savour a hoard: on the standard interpretations rasa is not consumed by being experienced.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: ed. and tr. W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, 1958)
references.note: The scholarly edition of the poem quoted above, with the Sanskrit, a literal translation, and notes that do not assume the reader accepts the tradition's claims. Brown is also good on the tangle of legends surrounding the poem's authorship, which is the same tangle that surrounds the Dravidian child of verse 75.

references.title: A Rasa Reader: Classical Indian Aesthetics
references.author: Sheldon Pollock (Columbia University Press, 2016)
references.note: The single best entry into the rasa debate in English: a thousand years of argument about Bharata's sūtra, in translation, arranged chronologically so that the positions can be seen developing. Read the introduction and the Abhinavagupta selections before deciding what rasajñā claims.

references.author: tr. Manomohan Ghosh (Asiatic Society / Chowkhamba, various reprints)
references.note: The standard complete English translation. Chapter 6 is the one to read for rasa; it is dry and taxonomic and gives no hint of the storm it caused, which is itself worth seeing before turning to the commentators.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma Stotram
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (Saregama / HMV)
references.note: The recording most reciters in South India learned from, and the most useful model for this particular verse, because the second line is exactly the kind of run of short p-names that inexperienced chanters rush. Listen to how the pace does not change between the long compounds of the first line and the five short names of the second.
